title: Detecting symmetry in designing heat exchanger networks
contribution: Group-theoretic characterisation of the symmetry in one temperature interval of the MILP transshipment model of heat exchanger network synthesis: streams with equal heat-capacity flow rates form symmetric groups whose direct product describes the interval (arXiv v1 of the FOCAPO/CPC 2017 paper).
problem_entry: Symmetry not characterised for HENS and not used by CPLEX 12.6 (toggling its symmetry feature leaves the tree unchanged); many equal-objective MILP transshipment optima posited to be symmetry (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Fix one temperature interval so continuous heat splitting no longer hides the structure; equal F(Cp) streams leave the residual change invariant and permute, giving S_nw per class and G(HP) x G(CP) per interval (Lemmas 2-3, Props. 4-7, Thm. 8, pp. 3-4).
assumptions: Constant equal temperature change per interval; hot-to-cold matches only, no HU-CU matches; sequential LP/MILP/NLP route rather than the simultaneous MINLP (pp. 1-3).
proof_devices: counting argument n^m for match configurations (Lemma 1, Appendix B, p. 6)
invariance of the residual change Delta R under swapping equal-F(Cp) streams (Lemma 2, Eq. 4, p. 4)
n! permutation count for the class symmetry group (Prop. 4, Appendix B, p. 6)
direct-product composition cited from Liberti 2012 / Costa et al. 2013 (Props. 6-7, Thm. 8, p. 4)
experiments: One minlp.org instance (Transshipment V1_5, 5 hot, 5 cold, 2 HU, 1 CU), GAMS model of Chen et al., CPLEX 12.6 solution pool; ten optimal solutions inspected to show swapped streams (pp. 4-5, Figs. 3-4).
positioning: Builds on Margot 2010, Liberti 2012, Costa et al. 2013 and Ostrowski et al. 2015 class-based symmetry; keeps the Papoulias-Grossmann formulation because Chen et al. 2015 reweighting gave no advantage (pp. 2-4).
writing: Short conference paper; 'for the first time' claim in the conclusion (p. 5); limits stated plainly (small test case, investment stage not examined, p. 5).
limits_future: Characterisation only; exploitation via symmetry-breaking or reweighted objectives left to future work; single small test case; investment-cost NLP not examined (p. 5).

method_links.note: Structure named and stated algebraically (steps 1-3), but no detector implemented, validated or exploited inside B&B (steps 5-6 absent).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: check the solver's own structure feature first
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Toggling CPLEX's symmetry feature does not alter the search tree, which motivates the study.

transferable: Toggle the commercial solver's symmetry handling and compare search trees as empirical motivation for a structure paper (p. 2).
Use the solver's solution pool to enumerate equal-objective optima and tabulate them so symmetric optima become visible (pp. 4-5).

quotes.text: State-of-the-art solver software CPLEX does not seem to use problem symmetry in the MILP transshipment model;
This paper has explored, for the first time, the symmetric structure of the HENS problem.

title: Bayesian multi-objective optimisation of neotissue growth in a perfusion bioreactor set-up
contribution: Closed-form expected hypervolume improvement for one black-box (GP-modelled) and one analytical objective, applied to bioreactor refreshment design and shown to beat NSGA-III on three test problems and the application.
problem_entry: Two conflicting objectives, one an expensive simulator and one an analytical cost; standard Bayesian MOO treats both as black boxes and weighted sums need a-priori weights and miss concave fronts (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Put a Dirac delta on the deterministic objective so the EHVI integral collapses to one dimension over rectangles below the current front, giving a closed-form differentiable acquisition (Eqs. 1-3, pp. 3-4).
assumptions: Two design variables (refreshment period, ratio); cost 1 + floor(504/r)*a with the floor ignored for the r-derivative; query-selection time negligible relative to evaluations (pp. 2, 5).
experiments: EHVI vs NSGA-III on Fonseca-Fleming, Schaffer, Kursawe and the TE problem; 10 initial points + 50 iterations, mean of 25 runs, GD/MPFE/volume ratio; single baseline, no variance (pp. 4-5, Table 1).
positioning: Extends Emmerich et al. 2008 EHVI; compares to genetic algorithms as 'the most common approach in literature' (pp. 1, 3).
writing: Calls its own win 'unsurprising' given few variables and iterations and states when GAs are preferable (p. 5).
limits_future: Advantage restricted to expensive evaluations and few variables; query time not counted (p. 5).

method_links.note: Single GA baseline at fixed settings, averages only, query time excluded: far from the auditor protocol (a 6-page conference application).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Known analytical objective kept exact (Dirac delta) inside the acquisition; only the simulator is GP-modelled.

transferable: Integrate out only the GP-modelled objective to get a closed-form, differentiable multi-objective acquisition (p. 4).
State the do-not-use regime (cheap evaluations, many variables -> GA) next to the win (p. 5).
coauthors: S. Olofsson (first), M. Mehrian, L. Geris, R. Calandra, M. P. Deisenroth

quotes.text: The computational time required to choose the next query point has not been taken into account since our focus is on applications where evaluating the black-box function is significantly more expensive than optimising for the next query point.
Whereas genetic algorithms can be preferable for applications with cheap function evaluations and higher number of design variables

title: Designing Energy-Efficient Heat Recovery Networks using Mixed-Integer Nonlinear Optimisation
contribution: One-page invited-talk abstract summarising two lines: automatic structure recognition for a simultaneous heat-exchanger-network MINLP demonstrated in ANTIGONE, and a parametric study of sparsity and the P/NP boundary in the standard pooling problem.
problem_entry: Energy efficiency of industrial heating and cooling (quarter of EU 2012 energy from industry, 73% of it heating/cooling); emphasis on large-scale industrial networks (p. 1).
key_idea: Recognise and exploit special structure of heat recovery inside a deterministic global solver; for pooling, relate sparse active topologies to a piecewise objective and to where complexity crosses P/NP (p. 1).
assumptions: Not stated beyond the p-formulation of the standard pooling problem (p. 1).
experiments: Not described beyond demonstrating impact on ANTIGONE and benchmarking large-scale cases against heuristics (p. 1).
writing: Abstract of an invited talk at an experimental-algorithms symposium.

method_links.note: States automatic recognition and exploitation of heat-recovery structure.
Structure exploitation judged by its impact on the ANTIGONE solver (stated only).

coauthors: R. Baltean-Lugojan, C. A. Floudas, M. Mistry

quotes.text: We automatically recognise and exploit special mathematical structures common in heat recovery.
Finally, the presentation explains the conditions under which sparsity vanishes and where the combinatorial complexity emerges to cross over the P/NP boundary.

title: Integrating Mixed-Integer Optimisation and Satisfiability Modulo Theories: Application to Scheduling
contribution: Replaces constraint programming by SMT (Z3) in Hooker's logic-based Benders decomposition for planning and scheduling: strongest method on minimum cost, weaker than pure MILP or SMT on minimum makespan.
problem_entry: Hybrid MILP/CP LBBD relies on bespoke CP constraints and may be poor without them; test SMT as the alternative subproblem solver (p. 1).
key_idea: Keep Hooker 2007 formulations, cuts and relaxations; use SMT unsatisfiable cores directly as the conflicting task sets in Benders no-good and makespan cuts; reformulate the pure-SMT model as generalised 2-D bin packing so constraints become pairwise (Eqs. 16-29, pp. 3-4).
assumptions: Hooker discrete-time planning/scheduling model with release/due times and cumulative resources; SMT as feasibility oracle with an iteratively tightened objective bound (pp. 2-4).
proof_devices: no new proofs; correctness from Hooker 2007 LBBD and mutual unsatisfiability of the core (p. 4)
experiments: Hooker's 335 instances, <18-task instances discarded (230 left); Gurobi 6.0.3 vs Z3 vs hybrid, 3600 s, performance profiles and average times on 'c' instances (pp. 4-6, Figs. 1-2, Tables 2-3).
positioning: Continues Jain-Grossmann 2001 and Hooker 2007 hybrid MILP/CP; positions SMT (De Moura-Bjorner) as the replacement for CP (pp. 1-3).
writing: Negative makespan result placed in the abstract and conclusion (pp. 1, 6); mechanism-level explanation of where each method learns (pp. 5-6).
limits_future: Hybrid weaker for makespan because the master learns only through cuts and per-facility subproblems block cross-facility learning (pp. 5-6).

method_links.note: Losses written into abstract and conclusion; written exclusion rule for toy instances with its reason.
Verdict split by objective class (cost vs makespan), but the component is a subproblem solver, not a relaxation inside B&B.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: swap one component of a published hybrid for a neighbour-community tool
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Hooker's LBBD formulations, cuts and relaxations held fixed; only CP replaced by SMT.

transferable: Hold a published decomposition fixed and change exactly one component to isolate its effect (p. 3).
Rewrite exponentially many subset constraints as pairwise disjunctions so infeasibility cores name small item sets (p. 3).
Discard toy instances from profiles with a stated reason (implementation bias) (p. 5).

quotes.text: But the hybrid MILP/SMT method is weaker than either MILP or SMT on a minimum makespan model.
Results for these toy test cases may be biased towards implementation opposed to algorithm performance.

title: Maximizing neotissue growth kinetics in a perfusion bioreactor: an in silico strategy using model reduction and Bayesian optimization
contribution: Reduces a 3D level-set/CFD neotissue growth model to spatially homogenised ODEs (about 10^5 times faster), reparametrises and sensitivity-tests it, and uses Bayesian optimisation on reduced and full models to find that frequent, large medium refreshments maximise growth (partner-led; Misener 6th of 7 authors).
problem_entry: Medium refreshment set by historical protocols; the 3D mechanistic model needs about 3 days per run, making optimisation almost intractable; evolutionary algorithms need too many evaluations (pp. 3, 5).
key_idea: Reduce first (PDE to ODE, piecewise-linear shear/curvature fits, GA-fitted parameters, Sobol sensitivity), then optimise with BO, and cross-check the optimum on the full model and against experiments and literature (pp. 4-19).
assumptions: Spatial heterogeneity irrelevant for the culture-strategy decision; Michaelis-Menten uptake; instantaneous refreshment; one averaged parameter set for all triply periodic scaffolds (pp. 5, 9, 21-22).
experiments: Reduced vs 3D on five scaffolds, comparison with hPDC culture data, BO at day 7 and day 21 on both models; 3D BO stopped after about 30 evaluations and augmented by hand-picked samples (pp. 14-19).
positioning: Positions BO against evolutionary algorithms for expensive simulators and cites Misener et al. 2014 RBC bioreactor optimisation as precedent (pp. 3-4, 20).
writing: First-of-its-kind pipeline claim (pp. 4-5); limits stated in the discussion (p. 20); a caption/text inconsistency (Fig. 4 G10 vs text G7, pp. 16-17).
limits_future: Homogenisation loses spatial mechanisms; no cost objective (multi-objective follow-up announced); averaged parameters lower maximum filling from 88% to 83% (pp. 19-22).

method_links.note: Optimum cross-checked across two models and literature, but the 3D BO is a single truncated run with manual samples.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: reduce the simulator until rigorous optimisation fits, then cross-check on the full model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: PDE-to-ODE reduction (2 s vs 3 days), BO on both, optima compared.

transferable: Validate a reduced model three ways: against the full model, against dedicated experiments, and by re-running the same optimisation on both (pp. 14-19).
Screen with a cheap early-time output (day 7) before full-horizon runs after checking that it predicts the final outcome (p. 17).
Report how much compute the full-model optimisation consumed and where it was stopped (p. 19).
coauthors: M. Mehrian (first), Y. Guyot, I. Papantoniou, S. Olofsson, M. Sonnaert, L. Geris (last)

quotes.text: Due to the high computational costs of the 3D model, we stopped the optimization process after around 30 evaluations, representing about 2 months of computation time.
Homogenizing the spatial variables reduces the mechanistic character of the model and does not address a number issues for which the spatial character is important.

title: Data-driven optimization of processes with degrading equipment
contribution: Integrates Levy-process degradation models from condition-based maintenance into a robust MILP for joint production and maintenance scheduling, proves a worst-case deterministic surrogate robust-feasible, estimates failure probabilities from data, and tunes the uncertainty-set size by Bayesian optimisation (arXiv v2 read).
problem_entry: Integrated maintenance-scheduling papers assume deterministic decay while CBM models are stochastic but single-unit; prior work fixes maintenance cost before optimisation so operating strategy cannot affect degradation (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Mode-dependent Levy increments as constraints, box uncertainty with a linear decision rule, Theorem 1 deterministic surrogate, logistic-regression frequency/Markov-chain estimators of failure probability, and BO over the set-size parameter alpha minimising cost plus expected failure cost (Eqs. 5-16, pp. 6-16).
assumptions: SMAX threshold failure and AGAN reset; piecewise-constant operating modes; uncertainty revealed once; independent increments (box set); at most one failure per unit in the horizon (pp. 5-9, 16).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: explicit construction of decision-rule coefficients (Eq. 11) and constraint-by-constraint check using nonnegative increments (p. 9; Appendix B, pp. 32-33)
robust counterpart via the Lappas-Gounaris affine decision-rule reformulation (p. 8; Appendix A not read)
experiments: Five STN instances, Pyomo + CPLEX 12.7.1; robust vs surrogate 25 runs each; estimator RMS/out-of-bound metrics against rolling-horizon solutions and an a-priori bound; BO vs random search, 5 runs; MIT-licensed code (pp. 20-29).
positioning: Bridges CBM degradation modelling and PSE integrated scheduling; extends Biondi et al.'s STN; contrasts with Yildirim et al. and Basciftci et al. (pp. 2-4, 17).
writing: Five bulleted contributions (p. 4); explicit scope sentences after the theorem and the surrogate comparison (pp. 9, 23).
limits_future: Box sets ignore correlation; complex sets need the full robust problem; estimators are imperfect upper bounds (up to 48% of points above); costs noisy from non-optimal solves (pp. 9, 21-27).

method_links.note: alpha parameterises a family from deterministic (0.5) to fully robust (0); the parameter is then removed from the user by an outer BO on expected cost.
Estimators checked against independent rolling-horizon simulations and a published a-priori bound; repeated runs, random-search control, public code.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: prove the cheap surrogate feasible, measure the rest
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 1 guarantees feasibility only; the surrogate's cost and gap are measured against the robust model.

transferable: Turn a robustness parameter into a one-dimensional expensive black-box problem (expected total cost vs alpha) and solve it by BO (pp. 15-16).
Prove robust feasibility of a worst-case surrogate by constructing the decision-rule coefficients explicitly (p. 9; pp. 32-33).
Grade a probability estimator as an upper bound with overall RMS, fraction of points above the bound, and RMS of those points (Eqs. 21a-c, p. 26).
Train a cheap surrogate for long horizons from short-horizon solves on Latin-hypercube demands (pp. 19-20).
coauthors: J. Wiebe (first), I. Cecilio (Schlumberger Cambridge Research)

quotes.text: Theorem 1 only guarantees solution feasibility, not optimality.
Noticeably, none of these authors make use of the wealth of knowledge regarding degradation modeling and inference from data available from the CBM literature.

title: Satisfiability modulo theories for process systems engineering
contribution: Position-and-testbed paper proposing SMT for process systems engineering via three testbeds: SMT-core-based algorithms (incl. a branch-and-bound with push-back symmetry cuts) for 2-D bin packing, unsatisfiable cores for cut generation and model debugging, and SMT-based MINLP solvers (ManyOpt).
problem_entry: PSE and computer science developed logic/optimisation hybrids separately; a strengths table shows SMT and MINLP are complementary (pp. 1-2, Table 1).
key_idea: Use SMT as a feasibility oracle whose unsatisfiable cores drive cuts, branching and symmetry handling (ascending algorithm, SMT-BB, Lemmas 1-2), and as a debugging and warm-starting tool (pp. 5-13).
assumptions: MINLP with inferable finite bounds and finite images; 2BP oriented and free cutting; ManyOpt limited to polynomial nonlinearities with exact rational arithmetic (pp. 2, 5, 11, 13).
proof_devices: Lemma 1 push-back cuts preserve the best objective: contradiction via an explicit bin-permutation map (pp. 7-8)
Lemma 2 identical items may also be pushed back: bin-swap map (p. 8)
dominance filtering: an unsatisfiable item set dominates its supersets (p. 6)
experiments: 500 Berkey-Wang 2BP instances, CPLEX 12.7, Gurobi 6.0.3, Z3 4.5.1, one thread, 1 h; time and heuristic performance profiles, per-class solved counts, Pisinger-Sigurd 'can solve' line; ManyOpt warm-start demos on prob03 and haverly (pp. 8-13).
positioning: Reviews disjunctive programming, GDP, MLLP, optimisation modulo theories and LBBD (pp. 3-4); distinguishes rigorous (ManyOpt) from complete (ANTIGONE) methods in Neumaier's sense (p. 13).
writing: Purpose stated as showing broad applicability (p. 1); §3.5 reuses S155's LBBD paragraph almost verbatim (p. 4); concessions on speed and scope (p. 13). Example 1's stated solution x1 = 5 violates its own x1 <= 1 conjunct (p. 3, own check).
limits_future: About half the 2BP instances solved; small-item classes hard for all; SMT polynomial-only; ManyOpt frequently slower than state-of-the-art MINLP solvers; warm starting not guaranteed to help (pp. 8-13).

method_links.note: Bespoke Pisinger-Sigurd method shown as a 'can solve' line; ManyOpt's slowness conceded (step 7).
Per-class solved counts expose where SMT-BB loses and why; one-thread limits for all solvers.
Bin-permutation symmetry and dominance exploited through logic-solver cores, not a detector inside a global MINLP solver.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: unsatisfiable core as a debugging instrument
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Filtered core of 7 constraints exposes a local cut not removed when switching branches.

transferable: Debug a B&B implementation by asking an SMT solver for the unsatisfiable core of a node known to be feasible, after filtering trusted constraints (pp. 9-10).
Promote local cuts to global ones by adding the fixing item as an antecedent for sibling branches (p. 8).
Demonstrate warm starting by counting oracle calls warm vs cold after adding one constraint (p. 13).
Plot a specialised method's solved count as a 'can solve' line to show the gap to bespoke methods (p. 8).
coauthors: M. Mistry (first), A. Callia D'Iddio, M. Huth

quotes.text: The purpose and novelty of this paper is to show the broad applicability of SMT to PSE.
ManyOpt is frequently slower than state-of-the-art MINLP solvers, but it offers the trade-off of a completely different method to address the problem.

title: Stem cell biomanufacturing under uncertainty: a case study in optimizing red blood cell production
contribution: Framework for stem-cell bioreactor design under uncertainty (high-fidelity models, sensitivity of the optimiser, global superstructure optimisation, robust optimisation, NPV analysis) applied to a dual hollow fibre red-blood-cell bioreactor: robust optimum $383 vs nominal $277 per unit, with NPV price targets.
problem_entry: The earlier nominal global optimum ($277/unit) ignored uncertainty, so its design decisions could not be checked; cell therapy adds kinetic, spatial, temporal and uncertainty requirements absent in petrochemical optimisation (pp. 2, 10).
key_idea: Six-component toolkit applied in a fixed recipe; convert model-form uncertainty into parameter ranges or a bounded cost shift (Krogh vs CFD; alternative hematopoiesis model moves $277 to $306 with unchanged design); then worst-case robust optimisation and NPV scenarios (pp. 2-10).
assumptions: Strict uncertainty with ranges and no distributions, hence worst case; 30 parameters at 50-150% of nominal; model kept near 200 variables for 300 s global solves; NPV assumptions (i)-(v) (pp. 5, 7, 9).
experiments: Computational: one- and two-parameter sensitivity of the global optimum, CFD stress test of the Krogh approximation, model swap, robust optimum and NPV scenarios at $800/$500/$225 (pp. 7-10).
positioning: Transfers superstructure and robust optimisation from heavy industry to stem-cell bioprocessing; claims neither had been applied there (p. 10).
writing: Futures-issue article; abstract says robustness costs about 15% while Results give $277 -> $383, about 38% (pp. 1, 8).
limits_future: Worst-case estimate pessimistic, more data needed for reasonable uncertainty rules; $500/unit target requires better cell flux through ceramic fibres (pp. 8, 10).

method_links.note: Abstract's robustness price (about 15%) does not match the Results figure ($277 -> $383, about 38%); an internal-consistency check of the kind Method 5 applies to competitors would flag it.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: fold model-form error into parameter ranges or a bounded cost shift
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: CFD stress-test of the Krogh approximation and an alternative hematopoiesis model re-solved to bound the cost effect.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: sensitivity of the optimiser, not the simulator
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Shadow prices rejected because of discrete design choices; sensitivities computed on the global optimum.

transferable: Budget a sensitivity study by counting optimisation runs (435 pairs x 4^2 level combinations x 300 s = 24.2 CPU days; 902.2 for triples) before choosing a Morris-style screen (p. 4).
Bound model-form error by re-solving with a plausibly pessimistic alternative model and reporting the change in optimum and decisions (p. 8).
Report how robust decisions differ from nominal ones, not only the cost (p. 8).
Close with an NPV scenario table that turns the optimum into a price target and names the physical bottleneck (p. 10).
coauthors: M. C. Allenby, M. Fuentes-Gari, K. Gupta, T. Wiggins, N. Panoskaltsis, E. N. Pistikopoulos, A. Mantalaris

quotes.text: Using robust optimization, the nominal price for a unit of RBC increases from $277 to $383.
we cannot tie ourselves to a single uncertainty analysis method; we want to build consensus between disparate analysis types.
